newsitem.title: MEXICO: Army role in Mexico drug fight seen paying off.
newsitem.headline: Army role in Mexico drug fight seen paying off.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo's risky decision to deploy the Mexican army at the front line of the drug war is starting to pay off, political analysts said on Tuesday.

They point to Monday's announcement by authorities that they had arrested a general for attempting to bribe another general into turning a blind eye to rampant drug trafficking on the U.S.-Mexican border.

The good news was that Gen. Jose Luis Chavez Garcia, Zedillo's hand-picked delegate to run the Attorney General's Office in Tijuana, had rejected a $1 million-a-month bribe from rogue Gen. Alfredo Navarro Lara.

"That's a good sign," said Jeffrey Weldon, a political scientist at Mexico's Autonomous Technical Institute. "It shows that there is some corporate responsibility in the military that works well sometimes. One million dollars is a lot of money to turn down."

In his first court appearance on Monday, the arrested general claimed he was forced by the notorious Tijuana-based Arellano Felix brothers, leaders of the Pacific cartel, to offer the bribe or face death for himself and his daughter.

Still, analysts said Zedillo's gambit of using the army to fight drugs remains a risky one, largely because it could corrupt one of the few government institutions whose image has not been sullied by perceptions of vast corruption.

"That is a danger the army faces," said Raul Benitez, a military affairs specialist at the Autonomous University of Mexico. "But this case is positive because it shows they are watching and that corruption will be firmly punished."

At U.S. urging, Mexico has been granting a higher anti-drugs profile to the armed forces in recent months, in large measure because of rampant corruption in the Attorney General's Office, which used to control the drug war alone.

Army troops have been deployed along key drug-trafficking routes, especially in the north of Mexico. But the move appeared to have backfired last month when a general appointed as the nation's top anti-drugs official was arrested on charges of taking bribes from a leading drug kingpin.

The Tijuana arrest is better news for the Mexican and U.S. governments, Weldon said. It also led a political satire column in the Mexico City daily Reforma to recall a famous quotation from a Mexican revolutionary leader early this century. "Alvaro Obregon's phrase that no general can resist a 50,000-peso barrage is no longer true," the column said.
